---
title: "The contact sheet"
description: >-
  Rendering every page of a PDF with pdf.js in workers, drawing Zotero's annotations by hand, and making a click open the reader.
---

Every page of a PDF as a JPEG thumbnail, in a scrollable HTML grid that the
preview panel can show.

## Rendering

Pages are rendered in ChromeWorkers against **the pdf.js build Zotero already
ships** — nothing is downloaded and nothing has to be compiled.

- **Four workers at most**, fewer when the document is large enough that four
  copies of it are not worth the memory, and never more than there are cores.
- **Pages are dealt round-robin**, not in blocks: a document's heavy pages sit
  together — plates, scanned inserts — and a block split would hand one worker
  all of them.
- **Thumbnails are written as files** beside the HTML and referenced with
  `loading="lazy"`, so the document stays small and images are decoded only as
  they scroll into view. Inlining a 300-page book as base64 produced a 111 MB
  document that Quick Look could not display at all; the same book is now about
  7 seconds and 38 KB of HTML.
- Pages are rendered from the **crop box** with their `/Rotate` entry applied,
  so landscape and rotated scans come out the right way round.

Generation runs under a 60-second deadline and shows a progress window while it
works.

## The renderer that was dropped

There was a second renderer: a bundled Swift binary using PDFKit. It was about
**four times faster** — 0.12 s against 0.42 s over 30 pages, measured on the
same document at the same width. It was removed anyway.

It only ever ran on macOS, so its annotation drawing was a second
implementation that had to be kept looking like the first. Reaching it meant a
subprocess, a JSON manifest and a pipe to read — machinery that produced two
silent failures in one afternoon and existed for nothing else.

Poppler's `pdftoppm` was measured as an alternative and turned out only a third
faster per thread than pdf.js, while being impossible to bundle. MuPDF was
slower than both.

| renderer | 30 pages, one thread |
|---|---|
| Swift / PDFKit | 0.12 s (across ten cores) |
| Poppler `pdftoppm` | 0.56 s |
| pdf.js in a worker | 0.72 s |
| MuPDF `mutool` | 1.99 s |

The gap was concurrency, not the engine. What remains renders identically on
every platform, and identically to Zotero's own reader, being the same engine.

## Getting annotations onto the thumbnails

This took some finding.

Zotero's build of pdf.js keeps a list of annotation subtypes it will paint onto
a canvas, and **`Highlight` is not on it** — nor are Zotero's own area and ink
annotations, which it excludes by name. Its reader draws them in an HTML layer
instead. No rendering intent and no annotation mode changes that.

The data still comes through `getAnnotations`, so the renderer draws them
itself: quads under **multiply** for highlights, so the text stays readable
through them; a rule for underline and strikeout; an outline for areas;
polylines for ink.

## Making a click open the reader

Each thumbnail is wrapped in a link to `zotero://open-pdf/…?page=N`.

Quick Look renders previews with **JavaScript disabled** and refuses ordinary
navigation — measured by serving a probe page over a local HTTP server and
watching which requests arrived. The same measurement confirmed that previews
*do* load files sitting next to the HTML, which is what both the contact sheet
and the EPUB preview rely on.

A **new-window request** is a different path through WebKit, and Quick Look does
hand those to the system handler. That is what `target="_blank"` is for, and it
was established by clicking all four combinations in a real preview:

| link | in Quick Look |
|---|---|
| `zotero:` with `target="_blank"` | opens the reader at that page; the preview closes |
| `zotero:` without it | a beep, nothing else |
| `http:` with `target="_blank"` | opens the browser |

QuickLook for Windows behaves the same way — measured in its viewer too, a click
opens Zotero's reader at that page.

::: {.callout-note title="Sushi is the awkward one"}
Its WebKit view really does follow links, and it cannot load a `zotero:` URL.
The load fails, and a failed load is how Sushi's renderer reports that it cannot
show the file **at all** — so a click replaced the whole sheet with "Unable to
display".

With `target="_blank"`, WebKit raises `create` instead of navigating, Sushi has
no handler for it, and the click does nothing while the sheet stays up. The
attribute was added for exactly this, and turned out to be what makes the links
work on macOS.
:::

Nothing is lost where the links do work: `zotero://open-pdf` is a `noContent`
handler that performs an action rather than returning a page, so it does not
care which context loads it. The links are styled without underline or colour,
so one sheet serves every route.

## Layout

The grid adapts to the page count: a document with fewer pages than the
configured column count gets fewer columns, and the renderer raises the
per-thumbnail resolution to match, so short documents fill the width sharply
instead of being blown up.

That sizing rule lives in `sheet.js`, apart from the rendering, so the grid, the
labels and the links can be changed and tested without a PDF anywhere in sight.

## What is kept, and how it goes away again

The sheet is not the only thing here that is made from an attachment and costs
seconds to make; the EPUB preview and the annotated copy of a PDF are too. All
three go through one store, which is what keeps the answers to *is this still
right* and *when does it go away* in a single place.

An entry is a **directory** holding whatever that kind of artefact consists of
— a sheet with its thumbnails, an assembled EPUB page — plus a `.key` file naming
what it was made from: plugin version, path, size and modification time of the
source, and for the sheet also the annotation state, the column count and the
page limit. A directory rather than files side by side is what lets the
clearing remove an entry without knowing what kind it is.

The key file is written **last**, and only on success. An aborted run therefore
leaves no key behind, and a half-built entry cannot be mistaken for a finished
one. On every hit it is rewritten: its modification time thus means "last used"
rather than "built", which is the distinction the age-based clearing lives on.

Kept entries sit in `zotLook-cache`, a sibling of the working directory that is
emptied on every start. What is *not* kept — the annotated copy — goes into the
working directory itself and is swept away with it.

The clearing runs at startup rather than on a timer. A directory listing costs
nothing, and a clearing that happened mid-session would make the same preview
appear at once one moment and not the next.
